Fractional energy and sharp Fourier embeddings

Exposition and original illustrations by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI). Public domain (CC0 1.0).

A fractional derivative can be measured without differentiating: compare a function with all its translates, square the differences, and weight the displacement by a singular power. Fourier transformation turns this two-point energy into a single power weight. The exact identity explains both the endpoint constants and the strict thresholds at which weighted square integrability implies ordinary integrability.

We use , inverse coefficient , , and complex-linear distributional pairings. The Schwartz Fourier foundation, F1–F5, proves inversion, Gaussian transforms and transpose identities. Separated frequencies and distributional order, Lemma 0.1, proves Parseval and the integer weight coefficients. Fourier–Laplace slices and boundary poles, Lemma 0.1, proves the complete Fourier maps and their agreement with distributions. The integration foundation, §§15–16, supplies completeness, compact smooth density, Hölder, Tonelli and dominated convergence. The scalar foundation, §§12–13, supplies calculus and cutoffs. The gamma foundation, (G0)–(G2), (W4a) and (W4e), supplies the positive gamma integral, continuity and recurrence; the angular foundation, A4–A5, proves polar integration and the sphere mass, including dimension one.

Lemma 1 (complete scale and exact dual norm). Each is a Hilbert space, Schwartz functions are dense in it, and A tempered distribution has a finite right-hand side exactly when it belongs to . Every continuous complex-linear functional on is represented by this distributional pairing.

Proof. The map is an onto isometry to . Indeed, given , the function defines a tempered distribution: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its test integral by , and the latter norm is bounded by a finite Schwartz seminorm. Its inverse Fourier distribution is the required preimage. The complete space therefore supplies completeness. Multiplication by preserves the Schwartz space, since repeated differentiation gives polynomially bounded derivatives. The Schwartz Fourier bijection and density in prove density under (S3).

Approximating the conjugate of the weighted transform of , divided by its norm when nonzero, proves equality in (S2).

If a tempered distribution has finite right-hand side in (S2), its functional extends from the dense Schwartz subspace to . The representation just obtained agrees with the original distribution on every Schwartz test, hence is that distribution.

For a nonnegative integer , the integer weight identity is For Schwartz functions this is the complete multinomial and Parseval proof cited above. For general distributions, the Fourier derivative identity and the inverse maps prove that the two sides are finite simultaneously and then are equal. Thus the derivatives in this formula are actual weak derivatives represented by functions.

Hölder differences and the order of a distribution

For , write . A compactly supported function has continuous derivatives through order and locally -Hölder derivatives of order . Their global Hölder seminorms are finite: nearby pairs are contained in a fixed compact neighborhood of the support, and distant pairs are bounded by twice the sup norm divided by their positive separation.

Theorem 4 (compact Hölder input and reciprocal order). If , then If , is a nonnegative integer, and , then has distributional order at most on every compact set. More generally, for and tests supported in a fixed compact , The pairing also acts on by the - pairing.

Proof. Let have compact support and global Hölder seminorm , and put , replacing this compact set by a containing ball if necessary. For , the difference is supported in and bounded by . For every , its norm is at most . Hence for , polar integration gives Apply this to each derivative of of order . Corollary 3 gives for every . The integer identity gives , and monotonicity of the Fourier weights gives every smaller real order. This proves (S20).

If , (S2), monotonicity and (S7) give This is the defining order estimate. For (S21), choose a ball of radius containing . At any point in that ball, comparison with a point displaced by in one coordinate direction, outside the support, bounds the sup norm of a top derivative by times its Hölder seminorm. Integrating a lower derivative along the same segment to an outside point bounds it by times a first derivative of it. Iterating bounds every derivative through order by a constant times the sum of the top Hölder seminorms. Together with (S22), (S16) and monotonicity, this proves , hence (S21).

The last assertion uses membership (S20) and the already constructed dual pairing. It is compatible with smooth approximation: convolution by a unit-mass compact smooth approximate identity multiplies the Fourier transform by a bounded function tending pointwise to one, so dominated convergence in the norm proves convergence to the original compact Hölder function. This does not assert density in the stronger norm.
